analysis.one_liner: Diverts a fifth of Social Security payroll taxes into personal stock-and-bond accounts while raising the retirement age.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on November 14, 2002, three weeks before the 107th Congress ended, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let workers redirect roughly a fifth of their Social Security payroll tax into personal retirement accounts invested in stock and bond index funds, while reducing their guaranteed Social Security benefit by the value of the money moved. It would have gradually pushed the full retirement age past 67, trimmed the traditional benefit formula, and required the Treasury to cover the diverted taxes from general federal revenues. It also bundled in smaller sweeteners: a refundable credit for low earners, a higher benefit for widows and widowers, extra earning years credited to caregivers, and tax credits for long-term care premiums and for families caring for elderly parents.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who opt to participate would own accounts that pass to their estates at death and could earn stock-market returns instead of the current formula's growth; low-income workers would get a $300 refundable deposit ($150 for those earning $25,000-$35,000); widows and widowers would get a benefit increase; caregivers and families supporting elderly parents would get tax credits; and the mutual fund and investment management industry would gain a vast new stream of mandated savings to manage for fees. Taxpayers who use IRAs and employer pensions would keep the larger 2001 contribution limits permanently.

how_it_helps.text: Each participating worker's payroll taxes (about 20% of the combined employee, employer, and self-employment Social Security tax) would be matched dollar-for-dollar from the Treasury's general fund and credited to an Interim Investment Fund, then transferred to the worker's personal account once it reached a $2,500 minimum balance.

Account money would be invested in one of three portfolios held with investment managers under contract to the trustees: a default 60% stock / 40% corporate bond mix, or optional 40/60 or 80/20 mixes, all replicating broad market indexes.
Unlike Social Security, money left in a personal account at death would go to the holder's estate as a lump sum.
Participating low earners would receive a refundable credit of $300 (incomes $5,000-$25,000) or $150 (incomes $25,000-$35,000) deposited into their account from the general fund.
Participants could deduct 50% of up to $2,000 in voluntary account contributions even without itemizing deductions.

The bill would increase monthly benefits for widows and widowers, disregard additional years of low earnings for parents providing child care, and exempt disabled adult children from the family-maximum benefit reduction.

It would make the pension and IRA provisions of the 2001 tax law permanent, accelerate scheduled increases in IRA and pension contribution limits, and add tax credits for long-term care insurance premiums, for taxpayers caring for dependent parents at home, and for seniors maintaining a principal residence.
It would require the Social Security Commissioner to study and report on how individuals could opt out of Social Security coverage entirely.

analysis.who_pays: Workers would pay in the form of lower guaranteed benefits: the bill cuts the traditional benefit formula (a new bend point shrinking replacement rates by up to 17% for middle earners by 2016 and beyond) and each participant's benefit is reduced by the annuity value of the taxes moved into the account. The full retirement age would rise gradually past 67, and the early retirement age would rise too, so people would wait longer for smaller checks. The Treasury's general fund — meaning taxpayers — would shoulder the cost of matching every redirected tax dollar plus the low-income credits, with required transfers climbing from $21 billion in 2005 to $283 billion in 2011, while annual appropriations to the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund would be cut by roughly 20-22%. Account holders would bear market risk on balances that replace a portion of their guaranteed benefit.

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts guaranteed benefits twice: it adds a bend point that progressively shrinks replacement rates (up to 17% lower for middle earners initially eligible in 2016 or later) and separately reduces each participant's Social Security benefit by the annuity value of the payroll taxes diverted to the personal account.
It gradually raises both the full retirement age and the early retirement age, so workers would have to wait longer to claim a smaller benefit.

The scheme is expensive: the general fund must match every redirected tax dollar and pay the low-income credits, with statutory transfers rising from $21 billion in fiscal 2005 to $283 billion in fiscal 2011, during a period when the 2001 tax cuts had already turned surpluses into deficits.

Account balances invested in stocks and bonds would be subject to market swings, and the guaranteed benefit offset is calculated using annuity pricing assumptions, so workers retiring after a downturn would lock in permanently lower Social Security checks.

Participation is the default for workers under the program (opting out is possible only before retirement age and requires forfeiting the account back to the trust funds), meaning most workers would be enrolled in market risk whether or not they wanted it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine upside is ownership and bequeathability: account balances pass to heirs, and historically stocks have outearned the implicit return of a pay-as-you-go system. But the bill pays for those accounts by cutting guaranteed benefits, raising the retirement age, and committing hundreds of billions in general-fund transfers, while shifting market risk onto workers whose benefit offsets are fixed by annuity math at retirement regardless of how their accounts actually performed. The low-income credits and widow/caregiver provisions soften the blow for some groups but do not change the core trade: smaller, later guaranteed checks in exchange for accounts whose value depends on the market at the wrong moment. It is a substantial risk-shifting proposal dressed with targeted benefits, not a free lunch on solvency.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced three weeks before the Congress expired, went to the Ways and Means Committee, and died there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Smith (R-MI) introduced the Retirement Security Act on November 14, 2002.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which held jurisdiction over Social Security and tax law.
No other member of the House signed on; the bill finished with zero cosponsors.
The action history ends with the referral: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traditional Social Security stayed exactly as it was: no payroll taxes were diverted, no guaranteed benefits were cut, the retirement age did not rise, and the mutual fund industry did not gain the new account business. Because the bill died with no support and no vote, the status quo won by default.

for.name: Rep. Nick Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Retirement Security Act on November 14, 2002 and recruited no cosponsors before the Congress ended.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee markup; the bill's action history ends with its November 14, 2002 referral to his committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only recorded support was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan lineup can be measured.

industries.industry: Investment management and mutual fund companies
industries.note: The bill would make Secretary-approved regulated investment companies the mandatory holders of every personal account and would have the trustees contract outside investment managers for the interim fund, locking in a permanent, enormous stream of worker savings for the industry to manage for fees. Fee drag on account holders is a real cost, though the bill directs the Secretary to weigh management costs in approving funds.
A refundable tax credit for qualified long-term care insurance premiums would subsidize premiums, lowering the cost of coverage for seniors who buy it and expanding the insurers' customer base.

Roughly a fifth of Social Security payroll taxes would flow annually into broad stock indexes and diversified corporate bond portfolios, a large new source of demand for securities. The capital-market benefit and the worker risk exposure are two sides of the same mechanism.
